title: Two Editors Argue Over Whether Craft Survives Automation
script: Bagas: [agitated] Twenty years sharpening a sentence until it earns its place on the page, Ratna, and now a machine produces something serviceable in four seconds. Forgive me if I don't consider that progress.

Ratna: [measured] Serviceable, though, is doing a great deal of work in that sentence. Serviceable was never the standard you held yourself to, and it still isn't the standard your readers actually reward.
Bagas: [defensive] Maybe not yet. But the market has never particularly cared about the difference between adequate and exceptional, provided adequate arrives faster and costs considerably less.
Ratna: [challenging] That's a fairly bleak indictment of every editor who's ever hired you, then, since presumably someone along the way did notice the difference.

Bagas: [conceding] Fair, though I suspect that discernment is precisely the faculty being quietly hollowed out, an entire generation losing the palate to distinguish craft from its convincing imitation.

Ratna: [thoughtful] Perhaps. Or perhaps craft simply migrates, the way it always has, toward whatever the machine still can't touch: judgment, risk, the deliberate imperfection that signals a mind was actually present.
Bagas: [wry] You're describing a shrinking territory with remarkable optimism. Each year the machine annexes another province you'd previously called uniquely human.

Ratna: [gently] I'm not claiming the territory won't shrink. I'm claiming what remains becomes correspondingly more valuable, not less, precisely because scarcity is the thing markets do reliably reward.
Bagas: [uncertain] And if I'm wrong about my own scarcity? If what I mistake for irreplaceable judgment turns out to be replicable after all, given sufficient data?
Ratna: [honest] Then we adapt, grieving what deserves grieving, without pretending the grief itself constitutes an argument against the tide actually arriving.
Bagas: [reflective] That's a colder comfort than I was hoping for, coming from you specifically.
Ratna: [warmly] It's the only honest comfort available. The alternative, insisting the tide won't come, has never once kept anyone's feet dry.
Bagas: [wry] Fine. I'll keep sharpening sentences, then, on the theory that someone, somewhere, will still know the difference when it matters.

Ratna: [smiling] That's not nothing, Bagas. Most craftsmen throughout history have worked under exactly that uncertain wager, and plenty of their work outlived the tools that eventually replaced them.

quiz.question: What is Bagas's initial grievance?
options: He is being paid too little
A machine can now produce serviceable writing in seconds after his decades of craft
His editor rejected his latest piece
Ratna refuses to work with him
quiz.explanation: Bagas is troubled that a machine can produce serviceable writing in seconds after his decades spent perfecting sentences.

quiz.question: What does Ratna say 'serviceable' was never the standard for?
options: Ratna's own writing only
What Bagas held himself to, or what readers actually reward
The publishing industry as a whole
Machine-generated content
quiz.explanation: Ratna points out serviceable was never the standard Bagas held himself to, nor what readers ultimately reward.

quiz.question: What faculty does Bagas fear is being hollowed out?
options: Basic literacy
The discernment to distinguish craft from its convincing imitation
Typing speed
Interest in reading altogether
quiz.explanation: Bagas fears the discernment to tell genuine craft apart from convincing imitation is being quietly lost.

quiz.question: How does Ratna reframe the shrinking territory of human craft?
options: As proof that craft is already dead
As making what remains correspondingly more valuable, due to scarcity
As irrelevant to markets entirely
As something that will reverse itself soon
quiz.explanation: Ratna argues that as human territory shrinks, what remains becomes more valuable because scarcity is reliably rewarded.

quiz.question: What comfort does Ratna offer regarding the 'tide' of automation?
options: That it will never actually arrive
That grieving what deserves grieving is honest, but doesn't argue against the tide arriving
That resisting it is always successful
That craftsmen have never faced this before
quiz.explanation: Ratna says the only honest comfort is adapting and grieving appropriately, since denial has never kept anyone's feet dry.
